steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The fog came in on a Tuesday, rolling over the sea like breath on glass. From the lantern room at the top of Greyhook Light, Elias watched it swallow the horizon, then the reef, then the last shiver of sun. The ocean vanished. In its place: a blankness that moved.

He wound the clockwork of the lamp with the care of a ritual he no longer had to think about. The great Fresnel lens loomed around him, all curves and prisms, an enormous glass eye waiting for its pupil of flame. When he opened the fuel valve and set match to wick, the light swelled slowly, like something remembering how to live.

“On you go,” he murmured, as he did every night. “Let’s make ourselves useful.”

The beam caught, a spear of white pushed into the fog, and the machinery under the floor began its damp ticking rotation. Every twelve seconds, the light would sweep the invisible sea. Every twelve seconds, a faraway sailor would see Greyhook’s signature blink and know: rocks here, danger here, life if you keep your distance.

When he first came to the island, fifteen years before, Elias had believed the point of his job was to keep ships from dying. That was easy enough to understand. Now, alone with the fog and his routines, he suspected the lighthouse was as much about keeping him alive as anyone on the water.

He did his rounds. The habit was a path worn deeper than the steps themselves: check the lamp, the fuel, the vents. Check the glass for salt crust and spider webs. Down the spiral stairs to the watch room; note the weather in the log—“1900 hrs, fog thick, wind light, bell sounding at regular intervals.” Down again to the living quarters, where the kettle was always sitting just off boil, as if waiting had seeped into the metal.

On the wall by the little iron stove hung a picture of his wife, taken the summer before she died. Her hair was wrapped in a scarf to keep off the spray; laughs had wrinkled the corners of her eyes in the instant the shutter snapped. Elias did not look at it long nowadays. Too many years could turn a face into something else, something like accusation.

He poured tea, then went out onto the gallery that circled the lighthouse like a balcony around a throat. The foghorn on the lower platform was booming, low and mournful, its notes smudged by the damp air. The fog moved around him in slow folds; drops collected on his eyebrows and beard.

He listened.

Long ago, on other foggy nights, he had imagined that if he listened hard enough, he would hear the sea talk. Voices in the waves: sailors, perhaps, or the whales he had once seen breaching far offshore. He was older now, and less inclined to trust imagination, but the habit of listening had stayed. It was more useful than talking, on an island where no one answered back.

A bell clanged out there—a ship’s bell, not his own “gong” buoy to the south. Elias straightened. The sound came again, closer than it should have been.

“Too near,” he muttered.

He hurried down to the lower platform where the foghorn crouched like some hunched animal. Beyond the railing, the world was nothing but white. He could hear surf, louder than it should be for the tide.

Another bell. Then a voice calling, chopped to pieces by the fog.

“—light—where’s the—?”

Elias went back up, heart knocking harder than any climb could justify. The lantern room was a pool of brightness, the lens rotating with its measured grace. The beam reached maybe fifty yards before being eaten.

“Come on,” he said under his breath. “You’re burning. You’re doing your part. Let them do theirs.”

Out in the whiteness, the bell clanged again, urgently. The foghorn bellowed, dutiful and enormous. For a moment, the sound of the sea was everything—crash and suck and the strange whisper that came when water retreated over rock.

Then, faint through the fog, a new sound: the grinding, terrible shriek of iron on stone.

Elias closed his eyes.

He did what training demanded. He logged the time and the conditions, fired a flare into the murk in case it might be seen, rang the little handbell that would signal any nearby craft to reply. All the while, he imagined the shapes he could not see: a small coastal freighter, perhaps, feeling its way up the channel; a captain trusting a chart and a clock more than his ears; a crew jolted from sleepy routine into the sharp work of not dying.

After the noise came the voices. Even from the tower, Elias could hear them now: shouts, then screams, then language dissolve into pure sound. He could picture lifejackets ripped from racks, the ugly silver hiss of flares, the snap of cold water like a slap.

And he could not leave the tower.

That was the rule. In a storm, in fog, in emergency: keep the light going. The island had a small derrick and a boat, and Elias knew every inlet and muscle of the rocks by heart. But if he left and another ship came, blind in the white, and found only darkness on Greyhook—then his choice would have traded one unknown disaster for another.

“You stay with the lens,” his first keeper had told him. “You are the heartbeat. Don’t stop your heart because another one is faltering. That’s not mercy. That’s panic.”

He stayed. He listened to the chaos wear itself out. Human voices grew fewer, then thin. The sea did the rest of its vast, indifferent work.

Hours later, just before dawn, the fog thinned. Patches of sky appeared, not yet light but less black. Elias saw the wreck finally, a dark length humped at an ugly angle on the reef. Parts of it still clung together; other pieces floated loose nearby, bobbing like driftwood.

He kept the light turning until the grey of morning made it pointless. Then he turned the valve, quenched the mantle, and watched the glow die down to a small orange coal before winking out. The absence of the beam felt obscene.

Down on the rocks, in the growing light, he found three men alive.

They were clinging to a jag of stone, their faces raw with cold and salt. Elias shouted, threw them a line, winched them to the landing. One had a broken arm; all of them shook violently, muscles clenching under bruised skin. He half-carried them up to the keeper’s house, wrapped them in blankets, made soup with hands that did not quite tremble.

“You the light?” one asked hoarsely, teeth clicking against the rim of the mug.

Elias nodded.

“We never saw it,” another whispered. “Swear we never. Just the horn. Then…rocks.” His eyes were wide, not accusing but bewildered, as if a rule of the world had been broken and no one had told him why.

“The fog can blind it,” Elias said. “Cuts it down to a few boat-lengths. You might have been just outside the reach.”

“But you had it on?”

“All night.” He heard the defensiveness in his own voice and hated it. “It was burning.”

The first man pushed wet hair back from his forehead. “Then I owe you my life,” he said simply. “That horn and whatever of that light got through.” He glanced down at his shivering hands. “Could’ve been worse.”

Elias looked at the three of them and thought of the many it probably had been worse for. He said nothing.

The rescue boat came mid-morning, a steel hull that glittered as it cut through the last ghosts of fog. Men with practiced efficiency took the survivors and information and left forms to be filled later. One of them—a young officer with an expression too carefully blank—asked to see the log.

Elias showed him the neat columns, the times, the conditions. “Lamp lit at 1845, full intensity. Fog at 1900, horn begun at standard interval.”

“You didn’t leave your post,” the officer said, almost to himself.

“No.”

The young man nodded. “You did right.”

After they left, the island was quieter than usual. Even the gulls seemed subdued, wheeling high above the wreck. The ship would be there for days, maybe weeks, depending on what the company decided: salvage or abandonment. Eventually the sea would break it down; rust would lace its bones and claim it.

Elias climbed once more to the lantern room, though there was nothing to do there now. Sun had burned the last of the fog away. The sea below was an untroubled blue, the sort of mild autumn day that tourists loved in the villages along the coast.

He stood with his palms on the cool brass rail and looked out.

It was not the first wreck he’d witnessed from Greyhook, and it would not be the last. In the logbook, they took up surprisingly little space: a date, a line or two of description, a tally. It was the spaces between the ink that took up room inside him.

He reached out and touched the glass of the lens, as gently as one might touch a forehead.

“We did what we could,” he said quietly. “We always do.”

In the glass, his reflection looked back at him: an older man, beard gone more salt than iron, eyes seamed at the corners like the picture on his wall. Behind him, mirrored into bright fragments, the empty sky.

He remembered, suddenly, something his wife had said years ago, when a storm had kept them both awake and the light had swung its steady arc through rain like falling needles.

“It’s a kind of promise, isn’t it?” she had murmured, drowsy against his shoulder. “That every time they look up, it will be there. Even if nobody ever thanks you. Even if they never know your name.”

He had laughed then and kissed her hair. It had seemed a sentimental way to talk about a job with so much grease and soot in it.

Now, alone with the lens and the silence, Elias understood that she’d been right. The promise was not to save everyone. That was too big, too cruel a promise for any human to make. The promise was smaller and harder: to be there, doing your part, whenever someone needed you and even when they didn’t.

At dusk, he lit the lamp again. The wick caught with less fuss, as if it, too, knew the drill. Outside, beyond the horizon, ships moved along their invisible lanes, trusting charts and instruments and one another. Some here, some far away. None of them thinking very much about the man on the rock who wound the clockwork and polished the glass.

The beam began its rotation, twelve seconds for a full sweep, then again, and again. Elias listened to the faint click of gears, the distant beat of waves, the sigh of wind.

He settled into his chair, logbook open, pen at the ready. The night had its work; so did he. Every twelve seconds, the lighthouse sent its white pulse into the dark, saying the only thing it knew how to say:

Here. Here. Here.
